# Using Chainlink Local simulator in your Foundry project
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/local-simulator

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE
>
> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:
>
> ```solidity
> import {CCIPLocalSimulator} from "@chainlink/local@0.3.1/src/ccip/CCIPLocalSimulator.sol";
> ```

You can use Chainlink Local to run CCIP 2.0 in a localhost environment within your Foundry project. To get started quickly, you will use the
[CCIP Foundry Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-foundry). This project is a Foundry boilerplate that includes the Chainlink Local
package (V3, `v0.3.1`) and CCIP 2.0 examples (`Example01`-`Example10`) covering token transfers, Fast Transfers, programmable token transfers, and Cross-Chain Token (CCT) setup.

In local mode, the simulator delivers messages synchronously inside `ccipSend` and applies the CCIP 2.0 OnRamp and OffRamp message rules: finality, one token per message, no zero amounts, and receiver CCV config validation. Read [CCIP 2.0 behavior in local mode](/chainlink-local/learn/ccip-v2-local) for the full list of what is and is not enforced.

## Prerequisites

1. In a terminal, clone the [CCIP Foundry Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-foundry) repository and change directories. Clone without `--recursive` and initialize the submodules one level deep:

   ```shell
   git clone https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-foundry.git && \
   cd ./ccip-starter-kit-foundry/ && \
   git submodule update --init
   ```

2. Run `forge build` to compile the contracts:

   ```shell
   forge build
   ```

The kit pins `solc 0.8.26` with `evm_version = cancun` in `foundry.toml`. CCIP 2.0 contracts need Cancun opcodes, so keep that setting in your own project.

## Test token transfers

You will run a test that transfers tokens between two accounts using `ExtraArgsV3` with Fast Transfers (non-zero block confirmations). The test file `Example01.t.sol` is located in the `./test` directory. It runs the real `Example01` script (`script/examples/Example01.s.sol`) against the Chainlink Local simulator, so a regression in the script fails the test. The file contains four test cases:

1. **Transfer with native fees**: Transfers CCIP-BnM from the sender to a receiver EOA, paying the fee in native gas, and verifies the receiver was credited and the router collected the fee.
2. **Transfer with LINK fees**: Same transfer, paying the fee in LINK.
3. **Revert on zero block confirmations**: `blockConfirmations == 0` means default finality; the script requires `> 0` for Faster Than Finality.
4. **Revert on zero amount**: The CCIP 2.0 rules reject zero-amount token transfers.

For a detailed explanation of the test file, refer to the [Examine the code](#examine-the-code) section.

In your terminal, run the following command to execute the test:

```shell
forge test --match-contract Example01Test
```

Example output:

```text
$ forge test --match-contract Example01Test
[⠊] Compiling...
No files changed, compilation skipped

Ran 4 tests for test/Example01.t.sol:Example01Test
[PASS] test_revertsWhenAmountIsZero() (gas: 41283)
[PASS] test_revertsWhenBlockConfirmationsIsZero() (gas: 41309)
[PASS] test_transfersTokenToEoaPayingLinkFee() (gas: 1430441)
[PASS] test_transfersTokenToEoaPayingNativeFee() (gas: 1350710)
Suite result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped; finished in 2.54ms (1.81ms CPU time)

Ran 1 test suite in 6.09ms (2.54ms CPU time): 4 tests passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (4 total tests)
```

No RPC URLs are needed: `forge test` runs only the no-fork Chainlink Local tests.

## Examine the code

### Setup

To transfer tokens using CCIP, the test needs:

- The local chain selector
- The local CCIP router
- A test token contract (CCIP-BnM)
- A sender account (the broadcaster)
- A receiver account

The shared base contract `test/utils/LocalSimulatorTest.sol` deploys the simulator and exposes the router, LINK and BnM. The `setUp()` function is invoked before each test case to reinitialize all the variables, ensuring a clean state for each:

1. Initialize the [Chainlink Local simulator](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#cciplocalsimulator) contract and read its [`configuration`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#configuration):

   ```solidity
   simulator = new CCIPLocalSimulator();
   (uint64 selector, IRouterClient sourceRouter,,, LinkToken linkToken, BurnMintERC677Helper bnm,) =
       simulator.configuration();
   ```

   **Note**: The [`configuration`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#configuration) function also returns the destination router, WETH9 and CCIP-LnM contracts, which these tests do not use. Hence, there are commas in the return values.

2. The example scripts wrap their calls in `vm.startBroadcast()` with no argument, so inside a test the transaction sender is `DEFAULT_SENDER`. That account is exposed as `broadcaster` and must hold the tokens and ETH the script spends:

   ```solidity
   address internal broadcaster = DEFAULT_SENDER;
   ```

3. `Example01Test.setUp()` funds the broadcaster with CCIP-BnM and creates the receiver:

   ```solidity
   function setUp() public override {
       super.setUp();
       example = new Example01();
       receiver = makeAddr("receiver");
       ccipBnM.drip(broadcaster);
   }
   ```

### Test case 1: Transfer with native fees

The `test_transfersTokenToEoaPayingNativeFee` function tests the transfer of tokens to an EOA while paying the fee in native gas. Here are the steps involved:

1. Set the fee the local router charges and fund the broadcaster with native gas. The local router charges only what `router.setFee(...)` sets (default 0) and uses a mock message ID:

   ```solidity
   uint256 fee = 0.01 ether;
   router.setFee(fee);
   deal(broadcaster, 1 ether);
   ```

2. Record the sender's initial token balance, then run the `Example01` script with the router, chain selector, receiver, token, amount, gas limit, block confirmations and fee token:

   ```solidity
   uint256 senderBefore = ccipBnM.balanceOf(broadcaster);

   bytes32 messageId = example.run(
       address(router),
       chainSelector,
       receiver,
       address(ccipBnM),
       AMOUNT,
       EOA_GAS_LIMIT,
       BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS,
       address(0)
   );
   ```

   The constants used:

   ```solidity
   uint256 internal constant AMOUNT = 1e17;
   uint32 internal constant EOA_GAS_LIMIT = 0;
   uint16 internal constant BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS = 5;
   ```

   - `EOA_GAS_LIMIT` is `0` because the receiver is an EOA: there is no `ccipReceive` logic to execute. The sender is billed for the specified gas limit, not actual usage, so do not set a gas limit for token-only transfers.
   - `BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS` is `5` (any value `> 0`): this requests a Fast Transfer, delivered before full chain finality. `0` would mean default finality.

3. Inside the script, the `ExtraArgsV3` are encoded with the `EncodeExtraArgsOffchain` helper, and the [Client.EVM2AnyMessage](/ccip/evm/api-reference/v2.0.0/client#evm2anymessage) is built with the receiver, token amounts, extraArgs and fee token:

   ```solidity
   EncodeExtraArgsOffchain extraArgsEncoder = new EncodeExtraArgsOffchain();
   bytes memory extraArgs = extraArgsEncoder.encodeV3Basic(gasLimit, blockConfirmations);

   Client.EVMTokenAmount[] memory tokenAmounts = new Client.EVMTokenAmount[](1);
   tokenAmounts[0] = Client.EVMTokenAmount({token: tokenToSend, amount: amount});

   Client.EVM2AnyMessage memory ccipMessage = Client.EVM2AnyMessage({
       receiver: abi.encode(receiver),
       data: "",
       tokenAmounts: tokenAmounts,
       extraArgs: extraArgs,
       feeToken: feeTokenAddress
   });
   ```

   `encodeV3Basic` maps `blockConfirmations` to the `requestedFinalityConfig` with `FinalityCodec._encodeBlockDepth`. Read more about `extraArgs` formats in the [CCIP best practices](/ccip/evm/concepts/best-practices#using-extraargs).

4. The script quotes the fee, approves the router to spend the token, and sends. With `feeTokenAddress == address(0)` the fee is paid in native gas:

   ```solidity
   uint256 fee = IRouterClient(sourceRouter).getFee(destinationChainSelector, ccipMessage);
   vm.startBroadcast();
   IERC20(tokenToSend).approve(sourceRouter, amount);
   messageId = IRouterClient(sourceRouter).ccipSend{value: fee}(destinationChainSelector, ccipMessage);
   vm.stopBroadcast();
   ```

5. The test verifies the transfer: the receiver was credited, the sender was debited, and the router collected the fee. Because local mode delivers synchronously inside `ccipSend`, the assertions run immediately after the script:

   ```solidity
   assertTrue(messageId != bytes32(0));
   assertEq(ccipBnM.balanceOf(receiver), AMOUNT);
   assertEq(ccipBnM.balanceOf(broadcaster), senderBefore - AMOUNT);
   assertEq(address(router).balance, fee);
   ```

### Test case 2: Transfer with LINK fees

The `test_transfersTokenToEoaPayingLinkFee` function tests the same transfer paying the fee in LINK. The differences from the previous test case:

1. Fund the broadcaster with LINK from the simulator faucet instead of native gas:

   ```solidity
   simulator.requestLinkFromFaucet(broadcaster, 1 ether);
   ```

2. Pass the LINK token address as the fee token, so the script approves and pays in LINK:

   ```solidity
   bytes32 messageId = example.run(
       address(router),
       chainSelector,
       receiver,
       address(ccipBnM),
       AMOUNT,
       EOA_GAS_LIMIT,
       BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS,
       address(link)
   );
   ```

3. Verify the router collected the fee in LINK:

   ```solidity
   assertEq(link.balanceOf(address(router)), fee);
   ```

### Revert test cases

The remaining two test cases verify the CCIP 2.0 send-time rules the local router enforces:

1. `test_revertsWhenBlockConfirmationsIsZero` expects the script's own require message, because `0` means default finality, not a Fast Transfer:

   ```solidity
   vm.expectRevert("blockConfirmations == 0 means default finality; use > 0 for Faster Than Finality");
   example.run(address(router), chainSelector, receiver, address(ccipBnM), AMOUNT, EOA_GAS_LIMIT, 0, address(0));
   ```

2. `test_revertsWhenAmountIsZero` expects the zero-amount rejection:

   ```solidity
   vm.expectRevert("amount must be > 0");
   ```

## Next steps

- Send a data-only message to a receiver contract and see the local router enforce its CCV config and minimum block depth in the [receiver CCV config guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/data-messages-receiver-ccv-config).
- For the other test files in the `./test` directory (`Example03.t.sol` programmable token transfers, `Example04.t.sol` sender contract, `Example05.t.sol` manual execution path), see the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples).
- To learn how to use Chainlink Local in forked environments, refer to
  the guide on [Using the Chainlink Local Simulator in your Foundry project with forked environments](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/local-simulator-fork).

# Pool-based CCV requirements on AdvancedPoolHooks in forked environments
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/pool-based-ccvs-fork

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE
>
> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:
>
> ```solidity
> import {CCIPLocalSimulator} from "@chainlink/local@0.3.1/src/ccip/CCIPLocalSimulator.sol";
> ```

This tutorial walks you through testing pool-based Cross-Chain Verifier (CCV) requirements on `AdvancedPoolHooks`, using the [CCIP Foundry Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-foundry)'s Example 09 (CCT 04). You will deploy a `CrossChainToken` with an `AdvancedPoolHooks` hook and a BurnMint pool on forks of *Ethereum Sepolia* and *Polygon Amoy*, configure the hook to require a CCV for transfers, and observe the source OnRamp consult it outbound and the destination OffRamp verify with it inbound.

Pool-required CCVs are the one CCIP 2.0 feature that local mode cannot exercise at all: local mode has no token pools, so pool-required CCVs are not enforced. Only the fork tests run them against the real OnRamp and OffRamp.

## How pool-based CCVs work

A token pool can require specific CCVs for its transfers. When a pool requires CCVs:

- the source OnRamp consults the pool's `getRequiredCCVs(...)` outbound and calls each CCV's `getOutboundImplementation` and `forwardToVerifier` on the source chain
- the destination OffRamp resolves the same CCV addresses on the destination chain and calls `getInboundImplementation` and `verifyMessage` before releasing or minting tokens

Because the destination OffRamp resolves the same address, **a pool-required CCV must exist at the same address on both chains**. Real CCVs are CREATE2-deployed to matching addresses on each chain.

`AdvancedPoolHooks` exposes this through per-remote-chain CCV configs:

- `outboundCCVs` / `inboundCCVs`: base CCVs, always required for transfers to/from that chain
- `thresholdOutboundCCVs` / `thresholdInboundCCVs`: additional CCVs, required only when the transfer amount is at or above `thresholdAmountForAdditionalCCVs`
- `address(0)` in a base list means "use the lane defaults alongside the other listed CCVs"

Threshold CCV lists require non-empty base lists (use `address(0)` in the base list if you want defaults below the threshold). Duplicates within and across lists are rejected.

## Prerequisites

> **NOTE: Prerequisites**
>
> Complete the [CCT burn and mint tutorial](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/cct-burn-and-mint-fork) first: it covers
> the kit setup, the keystore, the fork profile, and the Example 06 deployment and lane-linking scripts this tutorial
> reuses. Example 09 continues the setup from Example 08 (token + hook + pool with `AdvancedPoolHooks`).

## Run the fork test

The kit's `test/fork/Example09.fork.t.sol` runs this flow against pinned forks of the live testnets. The file contains five test cases:

1. **Config storage**: `applyCCVConfigUpdates` stores the CCV config on both hooks.
2. **Both-sides consultation**: A transfer succeeds end to end while the source OnRamp consults the CCV outbound and the destination OffRamp verifies with it inbound.
3. **Threshold CCVs**: Threshold CCVs are required only at or above the threshold amount.
4. **Clearing**: Re-running the config script with empty lists removes the config.
5. **Validation**: Threshold CCVs without base CCVs revert with `MustSpecifyUnderThresholdCCVsForThresholdCCVs`.

In your terminal, run the following command to execute the test:

```shell
FOUNDRY_PROFILE=fork forge test --match-contract Example09ForkTest -j 1
```

Example output:

```text
$ FOUNDRY_PROFILE=fork forge test --match-contract Example09ForkTest -j 1
Ran 5 tests for test/fork/Example09.fork.t.sol:Example09ForkTest
[PASS] test_send_poolRequiredCCVIsConsultedOnBothSides() (gas: 2304798)
[PASS] test_send_thresholdCCVsAreRequiredAboveThresholdAmount() (gas: 4369395)
[PASS] test_setPoolCCVConfig_clearingWithEmptyListsRemovesConfig() (gas: 380961)
[PASS] test_setPoolCCVConfig_revertsWhenThresholdCCVsHaveNoBaseCCVs() (gas: 64126)
[PASS] test_setPoolCCVConfig_storesConfigOnBothHooks() (gas: 528563)
Suite result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped; finished in 2.19s (13.67ms CPU time)

Ran 1 test suite in 2.20s (2.19s CPU time): 5 tests passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (5 total tests)
```

## Examine the code

### Setup

The shared base contract `test/fork/utils/AdvancedPoolHooksForkTest.sol` extends the CCT fork setup: it deploys a `CrossChainToken`, an `AdvancedPoolHooks` hook and a BurnMint pool on both forks, and links the lanes, so each Example 08-10 test file only adds the hook feature it covers. The hook is deployed with `thresholdAmountForAdditionalCCVs = 1`, so threshold CCVs are effectively always required until you raise the threshold.

`Example09ForkTest.setUp()` adds the CCV. The test deploys a `CountingCCV` (a no-op CCV that counts consultations and verifications) once and makes it persistent, so it exists at the same address on both chains:

```solidity
vm.selectFork(sepoliaFork);
ccv = CountingCCV(_persistent(address(new CountingCCV())));
thresholdCCV = CountingCCV(_persistent(address(new CountingCCV())));
```

Real CCVs are CREATE2-deployed to matching addresses on each chain; the persistent test contract achieves the same property. Like the simulator's own CCVs, it performs no real verification.

### Configure the CCV on both hooks

The `Example09SetPoolCCVConfig` script wraps `AdvancedPoolHooks.applyCCVConfigUpdates`. The test requires the CCV for both outbound and inbound traffic on each side of the lane:

```solidity
_setCCVConfig(sepoliaFork, sepoliaHook, amoy.chainSelector, address(ccv));
_setCCVConfig(amoyFork, amoyHook, sepolia.chainSelector, address(ccv));
```

`test_setPoolCCVConfig_storesConfigOnBothHooks` then reads the config back from both hooks and asserts the CCV appears in the outbound and inbound lists.

### Observe the CCV consulted on both sides

`test_send_poolRequiredCCVIsConsultedOnBothSides` sends a default-finality transfer Sepolia → Amoy and routes it with `switchChainAndRouteMessage`, then asserts three things:

```solidity
_sendDefaultFinalityAndRoute(sepoliaToken, TRANSFER_AMOUNT);

// The transfer still succeeds end to end.
assertEq(_balanceOnFork(amoyFork, amoyToken, receiver), TRANSFER_AMOUNT);
assertEq(_supplyOnFork(amoyFork, amoyToken), destinationSupplyBefore + TRANSFER_AMOUNT);

// The source OnRamp consulted the CCV outbound (getOutboundImplementation + forwardToVerifier).
vm.selectFork(sepoliaFork);
assertEq(ccv.outboundConsultations(), 1, "source OnRamp did not consult the pool-required CCV");

// The destination OffRamp verified the message inbound (getInboundImplementation + verifyMessage).
vm.selectFork(amoyFork);
assertEq(ccv.inboundVerifications(), 1, "destination OffRamp did not verify with the pool-required CCV");
```

The counters prove the pool-required CCV participated on both chains: one outbound consultation on the source, one inbound verification on the destination.

### Threshold CCVs

`test_send_thresholdCCVsAreRequiredAboveThresholdAmount` configures base CCVs plus threshold CCVs, then moves the threshold around the transfer amount:

```solidity
// Raise the threshold above the transfer amount: only the base CCV is required.
_setThreshold(sepoliaFork, sepoliaHook, TRANSFER_AMOUNT + 1);
_setThreshold(amoyFork, amoyHook, TRANSFER_AMOUNT + 1);
_setCCVConfigWithThreshold(sepoliaFork, sepoliaHook, amoy.chainSelector, address(ccv), address(thresholdCCV));
_setCCVConfigWithThreshold(amoyFork, amoyHook, sepolia.chainSelector, address(ccv), address(thresholdCCV));

_sendDefaultFinalityAndRoute(sepoliaToken, TRANSFER_AMOUNT);

vm.selectFork(sepoliaFork);
assertEq(thresholdCCV.outboundConsultations(), 0, "threshold CCV consulted below threshold");

// Now lower the threshold to 1 wei: the same transfer amount requires the threshold CCV too.
_setThreshold(sepoliaFork, sepoliaHook, 1);
_setThreshold(amoyFork, amoyHook, 1);

_sendDefaultFinalityAndRoute(sepoliaToken, TRANSFER_AMOUNT);

vm.selectFork(sepoliaFork);
assertEq(thresholdCCV.outboundConsultations(), 1, "threshold CCV not consulted at/above threshold");
```

The same transfer amount flips between requiring and not requiring the threshold CCV as the threshold moves, on both the outbound and inbound side.

## Run the same flow on a live testnet

The kit's book chapter lists the script commands for the live-testnet flow: deploy the token, hook and pool on both chains (Example 08 steps), set the pool CCV config on both hooks with `Example09SetPoolCCVConfig`, send with the Example 06 sender, adjust the threshold with `Example09SetThresholdAmount`, and clear the config by re-running the config script with empty lists. See the [Example 09 chapter](https://smartcontractkit.github.io/ccip-starter-kit-foundry/examples/example09-cct04-pool-based-ccvs-on-advanced-pool-hooks.html) of the kit's book.

> **NOTE: Real CCVs**
>
> The starter kit does not deploy a real CCV; its tests use a counting no-op CCV. To try pool-based CCVs end to end on
> the live testnets, deploy your own CCV with the [CCV starter kit](https://docs.chain.link/ccip/ccv-starter-kit) and
> use its resolver address as the CCV address. Use the resolver address, not the committee verifier implementation: a
> pool that lists the implementation address reverts during the fee quote.

- Example 08 covers the sender allowlist on the same hook; see [Configure a sender allowlist](/ccip/evm/tutorials/cross-chain-tokens/configure-sender-allowlist-advanced-pool-hooks-foundry).
- For an index of every kit example and where its topic is documented, read the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples).

# Sending data to a receiver with CCV config in your Hardhat project
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/data-messages-receiver-ccv-config

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE
>
> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:
>
> ```solidity
> import {CCIPLocalSimulator} from "@chainlink/local@0.3.1/src/ccip/CCIPLocalSimulator.sol";
> ```

This guide walks you through the CCIP 2.0 receiver-side finality rules in local mode, using the [CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat)'s Example 02. You will send a data-only message to a `BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVs` contract with Fast Transfers, and see the local router reject it when the requested block confirmations fall below the receiver's minimum block depth.

The Example 01 guide covers a token-only transfer to an EOA, which is exactly the case that skips the receiver finality check. This guide covers the opposite case: a message with data and a receiver contract, where the local router reads the receiver's `getCCVsAndFinalityConfig` and enforces its allowed finality, reproducing the CCIP 2.0 OffRamp check. Read [CCIP 2.0 behavior in local mode](/chainlink-local/learn/ccip-v2-local) for the full rule list.

> **NOTE: Hardhat 3 required**
>
> Chainlink Local `0.3.x` does not compile under Hardhat 2. Hardhat 2 users stay on the `0.2.x` line (`npm install
>   @chainlink/local@0.2.9`).

## Prerequisites

Complete the [Hardhat local simulator guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator) first: it covers cloning the kit, `npm install`, and the `setupLocalSimulator` helper this guide builds on.

## Test data messages to a receiver with CCV config

The test file `Example02.test.ts` is located in the `./test` directory. It calls the real Example 02 task actions (`tasks/Example02.ts` and `tasks/helpers/SetBasicMessageReceiverWithCCVsMinBlockDepth.ts`) against the Chainlink Local simulator. The file contains nine test cases:

1. **Deploy**: The receiver is wired to the router and owned by the deployer.
2. **Deliver above the minimum depth**: A Fast Transfer with confirmations above the receiver's `minBlockDepth` is delivered.
3. **Deliver at the minimum depth**: Confirmations equal to `minBlockDepth` are also delivered.
4. **Deliver with default finality**: A message with `blockConfirmations = 0` is delivered even when no `minBlockDepth` is set.
5. **Deliver with a CCV config applied**: A receiver with required and optional CCVs still gates on `minBlockDepth`.
6. **Revert below the minimum depth**: Confirmations below `minBlockDepth` revert with `InvalidRequestedFinality`.
7. **Revert when the minimum depth is unset**: Without a configured depth, the receiver accepts finalized messages only.
8. **Argument validation**: The tasks reject a zero source chain selector and a zero receiver.

In your terminal, run the following command to execute the test:

```shell
npx hardhat test nodejs
```

Example output:

```text
$ npx hardhat test nodejs

Example02
  ✔ deploys the receiver wired to the router and owned by the deployer (644ms)
  ✔ delivers the message when confirmations are above the min block depth (285ms)
  ✔ delivers the message when confirmations equal the min block depth (347ms)
  ✔ delivers a message with default finality (0 confirmations) even when no min block depth is set (165ms)
  ✔ delivers the message when the receiver has a CCV config applied (223ms)
  ✔ reverts when confirmations are below the min block depth (141ms)
  ✔ reverts when the min block depth is unset, so only full finality is accepted (137ms)
  ✔ set-min-block-depth task rejects a zero source chain selector
  ✔ rejects a zero receiver

...
```

## Examine the code

### The receiver contract

`contracts/BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVs.sol` extends `BasicMessageReceiver` with a per-source-chain CCV and finality policy. Two settings matter for this guide:

- `setMinBlockDepth(sourceChainSelector, minBlockDepth)`: the minimum block depth the receiver accepts for Fast Transfers from that chain. `0` means the receiver requires default finality (fully finalized messages only).
- `getCCVsAndFinalityConfig(sourceChainSelector, sender)`: the CCIP 2.0 receiver interface the OffRamp calls for every message that is not a token-only transfer. The kit's receiver returns its stored CCV config and encodes `minBlockDepth` as the allowed finality with `FinalityCodec._encodeBlockDepth`.

### Setup

The `beforeEach` hook deploys the receiver through the same Ignition module the kit's book uses for live-testnet deployments, so the test exercises the real deployment path:

```typescript
s = await setupLocalSimulator()
const { basicMessageReceiverWithCCVs } = await s.connection.ignition.deploy(BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVsModule, {
  parameters: { BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVsModule: { routerAddress: s.router.address } },
})
receiver = await s.viem.getContractAt("BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVs", basicMessageReceiverWithCCVs.address)
```

The helper functions wrap the two task actions the test drives:

```typescript
const setMinBlockDepth = (minBlockDepth: number, sourceChainSelector = s.chainSelector) =>
  quietly(() => setMinBlockDepthAction({ receiver: receiver.address, sourceChainSelector, minBlockDepth }, s.taskHre))

const send = (blockConfirmations: number, overrides: { receiver?: string } = {}) =>
  quietly(() =>
    example02Action(
      {
        sourceRouter: s.router.address,
        destinationChainSelector: s.chainSelector,
        receiver: overrides.receiver ?? receiver.address,
        messageText: MESSAGE_TEXT,
        gasLimit: GAS_LIMIT,
        blockConfirmations,
        feeTokenAddress: ZERO_ADDRESS,
      },
      s.taskHre
    )
  )
```

The constants used:

```typescript
const MESSAGE_TEXT = "Hello CCIP 2.0"
const GAS_LIMIT = 200_000
```

`GAS_LIMIT` must be `> 0`: the receiver has a `ccipReceive` callback to execute, unlike the EOA receiver of Example 01.

### Deliver when confirmations meet the minimum depth

The `delivers the message when confirmations are above the min block depth` test case sets the receiver's minimum depth to `3` and sends with `5` confirmations:

```typescript
await setMinBlockDepth(3)

await send(5)

assert.notEqual(await receiver.read.latestMessageId(), `0x${"00".repeat(32)}`)
assert.equal(await receiver.read.latestSourceChainSelector(), s.chainSelector)
assert.equal((await receiver.read.latestSender()).toLowerCase(), s.broadcaster.account.address.toLowerCase())
assert.equal(await receiver.read.latestMessage(), encodeAbiParameters([{ type: "string" }], [MESSAGE_TEXT]))
```

Inside the send, the local router parses the `ExtraArgsV3` requested finality, sees the message has data (not a token-only transfer), and calls the receiver's `getCCVsAndFinalityConfig`. The receiver's allowed finality is `FinalityCodec._encodeBlockDepth(3)`; the requested `5` is at least that, so the message is delivered synchronously and the assertions read the receiver's stored state directly.

The `delivers the message when confirmations equal the min block depth` test case sends with exactly `3` confirmations and passes: the check is inclusive.

### Revert when confirmations fall below the minimum depth

The `reverts when confirmations are below the min block depth` test case sends with `2` confirmations against a minimum depth of `3`. The local router rejects the send with the same error the production OffRamp records:

```typescript
await setMinBlockDepth(3)

await expectInvalidFinality(send(2), blockDepth(2), blockDepth(3))
```

`expectRevertWithError` decodes the revert data and asserts the exact custom error and arguments. `blockDepth(n)` is the finality encoding of a block-depth request, `bytes4(uint32(n))`:

```typescript
const blockDepth = (n: number) => `0x${n.toString(16).padStart(8, "0")}`
```

The error carries both sides of the comparison: the requested finality (`0x00000002`) and the allowed finality (the receiver's minimum depth, `0x00000003`).

The `reverts when the min block depth is unset, so only full finality is accepted` test case shows the default: with no depth configured, the receiver's allowed finality is `WAIT_FOR_FINALITY` (`0x00000000`), so any Fast Transfer request reverts:

```typescript
await expectInvalidFinality(send(1), blockDepth(1), WAIT_FOR_FINALITY)
```

A message with `blockConfirmations = 0` (default finality) is still delivered in this state, which the `delivers a message with default finality` test case verifies.

### Deliver with a CCV config applied

The `delivers the message when the receiver has a CCV config applied` test case configures the receiver with required and optional CCVs through `applyCCVConfigUpdates`, then verifies the finality gate still applies on top:

```typescript
await receiver.write.applyCCVConfigUpdates([
  [
    {
      requiredCCVs: ["0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000a1"],
      optionalCCVs: ["0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000b1", "0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000b2"],
      sourceChainSelector: s.chainSelector,
      optionalThreshold: 1,
    },
  ],
])
await setMinBlockDepth(3)

await send(3)

assert.notEqual(await receiver.read.latestMessageId(), `0x${"00".repeat(32)}`)
await expectInvalidFinality(send(2), blockDepth(2), blockDepth(3))
```

Local mode has no CCV verifiers, so it cannot check quorum. It does validate the config itself (duplicate CCVs, `optionalThreshold` beyond the optional list length) the same way the OffRamp does, so a receiver configured this way is accepted by the router-side validation and keeps gating on the minimum block depth.

## Run the same flow on a live testnet

The kit's book chapter lists the task commands for the live-testnet flow: deploy the receiver with Ignition on the destination chain, set its minimum block depth with the `set-basic-message-receiver-with-ccvs-min-block-depth` task, then send the data message with the `example02` task. See the [Example 02 chapter](https://smartcontractkit.github.io/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat/examples/example02-hello-world-to-basic-message-receiver.html) of the kit's book.

## Next steps

- `Example03.test.ts` combines this receiver-side gating with a token transfer (data + tokens in one message).
- To see the receiver finality rules enforced by the real OffRamp instead of the local router, read the [forked environments guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator-fork).
- For an index of every kit example and where its topic is documented, read the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples).

# Using Chainlink Local to Test CCIP in Your Hardhat Project
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE

> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:

> ```

There are three guides to help you test Chainlink CCIP 2.0 in your Hardhat project using Chainlink Local - two for local mode and one for forked environments. The guides use the [CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat) (Hardhat 3), whose CCIP 2.0 examples (`Example01`-`Example10`) run as Hardhat tasks and Ignition modules on the Ethereum Sepolia → Polygon Amoy lane.

Read [CCIP 2.0 behavior in Chainlink Local](/chainlink-local/learn/ccip-v2-local) to understand what the simulator enforces in each mode, or the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples) for an index of every kit example.

## Guides

### Using Chainlink Local Simulator in your Hardhat project

This [guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator) helps you set up and run CCIP 2.0 in a localhost environment within your Hardhat project. It provides step-by-step instructions on :

- Cloning the
  [CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat)
- Installing necessary dependencies
- Running tests for token transfers between two accounts using `ExtraArgsV3` with Fast Transfers

Using the local simulator without forking is ideal for initial development and testing in an isolated environment.

### Sending data to a receiver with CCV config

This [guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/data-messages-receiver-ccv-config) covers the receiver-side finality rules in local mode: a data-only message to a `BasicMessageReceiverWithCCVs` contract, where the local router enforces the receiver's minimum block depth for Fast Transfers.

### Using Chainlink Local Simulator in your Hardhat project with forked environments

This [guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator-fork) extends your testing capabilities by demonstrating how to use the Chainlink Local Simulator in a forked environment. It includes instructions on:

- Setting up forks of real blockchain networks (Ethereum Sepolia and Polygon Amoy, a live CCIP 2.0 lane)
- Routing messages across forks with the Hardhat 3 JavaScript fork helper for every CCIP era
- Running the CCT fork tests (token and pool deployment, registration, Faster Than Finality gates)

Using the local simulator with forked environments is ideal for testing in a more realistic yet controlled setting.

# Using Chainlink Local Simulator in Your Hardhat Project - Forked Environments
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator-fork

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE
>
> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:
>
> ```solidity
> import {CCIPLocalSimulator} from "@chainlink/local@0.3.1/src/ccip/CCIPLocalSimulator.sol";
> ```

You can use Chainlink Local to run CCIP 2.0 in forked environments within your Hardhat 3 project. To get started quickly, you will use the [CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat).
The kit's `test-fork` directory contains fork tests for the CCT examples (`Example06`-`Example10`), which run the real Ignition modules and tasks against pinned forks of *Ethereum Sepolia* and *Polygon Amoy* (a live CCIP 2.0 lane) and route each message to the destination OffRamp with the Chainlink Local JavaScript fork helper (`@chainlink/local/scripts/CCIPLocalSimulatorFork.js`).

The helper routes messages for every CCIP era: pre-1.6 (`EVM2EVMOnRamp`), 1.6 and CCIP 2.0 (CCV-based lanes, which live testnet lanes run today). On CCIP 2.0 lanes the destination OffRamp selects the CCVs and executes the message through the permissionless `execute` entrypoint; CCV attestations are simulated with a synthetic no-op verifier.

## Prerequisites

This guide assumes that you are familiar with the guide [Using Chainlink Local Simulator in Your Hardhat Project](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator).
If not, please get familiar with it and run all the prerequisites.

Fork tests have three requirements beyond the no-fork setup:

1. **Node.js 22 and the `@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ethers` plugin**, which the JavaScript fork helper uses (`connection.ethers`). The kit already registers the plugin in `hardhat.config.ts`.

2. **Archive-capable RPC URLs for both chains.** A free-tier Alchemy or Infura endpoint works; public non-archive endpoints fail with "historical state is not available". Provide them as environment variables or in the Hardhat keystore:

   ```shell
   npx hardhat keystore set ETHEREUM_SEPOLIA_RPC_URL
   npx hardhat keystore set POLYGON_AMOY_RPC_URL
   ```

3. **The `production` build profile**: the token pools exceed the 24 KB contract size limit without the optimizer. The kit's `test:fork` script sets it.

The fork networks are defined in `hardhat.config.ts` with pinned blocks, so a fresh clone runs the same chain state:

```ts
sepoliaFork: {
  type: "edr-simulated",
  chainType: "generic",
  chainId: 11155111,
  forking: {
    url: configVariable("ETHEREUM_SEPOLIA_RPC_URL"),
    blockNumber: Number(process.env.ETHEREUM_SEPOLIA_FORK_BLOCK ?? 11_920_292),
  },
},
```

Override the pins for a run with `ETHEREUM_SEPOLIA_FORK_BLOCK` / `POLYGON_AMOY_FORK_BLOCK`, for example to check whether the live lane has drifted.

## Test a CCT transfer across a CCIP 2.0 lane

You will run the fork test for Example 06 (CCT 01: `CrossChainToken` + BurnMint pool). The test file `Example06.fork.test.ts` is located in the `./test-fork` directory. It deploys a custom token and pool on both forks through the kit's Ignition module, registers them in the live TokenAdminRegistry, links the pools, and sends token transfers across the Sepolia → Amoy CCIP 2.0 lane. The file contains seven test cases, including:

1. **Deploy**: Creates the token and pool and registers them on both chains.
2. **Configure lane**: Sets the remote token and pool.
3. **Send with default finality**: Burns on the source and mints on the destination.
4. **Send with Faster Than Finality**: Reverts until the pool opts in, then delivers after both pools opt in.

In your terminal, run the following command to execute the test:

```shell
npm run test:fork
```

Example output:

```text
$ npm run test:fork

Example06 (fork)
  ✔ deploy creates the token and pool and registers them (1962ms)
  ✔ configureLane sets the remote token and pool (1200ms)
  ✔ configureLane rerun replaces the existing config (1167ms)
  ✔ send at default finality burns on the source and mints on the destination (1338ms)
  ✔ send with Faster Than Finality reverts until the pool opts in (1328ms)
  ✔ send with Faster Than Finality delivers after both pools opt in (1441ms)
  ✔ check-finality-gates finds the registered pool (1105ms)

...

27 passing (36481ms)
```

## Examine the code

### Setup

The shared setup lives in `test-fork/utils/cctFork.ts`. To route messages across forks, the test needs:

- A fork connection for the source chain (Ethereum Sepolia) and the destination chain (Polygon Amoy)
- The chain details (routers, RMN proxy, registries) for both chains
- A sender account (the broadcaster, Hardhat wallet 0) and a receiver account

The `setupForks()` function:

1. Connects to both fork networks and wraps each connection in a `Fork` object with the chain details, the public client, the broadcaster, and a `taskHre` whose `connect()` returns that fork (for running the example tasks against it):

   ```typescript
   const sepolia = await connectFork("sepoliaFork", SEPOLIA)
   const amoy = await connectFork("amoyFork", AMOY)
   ```

   The chain details (routers, RMN proxy, registries) are copied from `@chainlink/local`'s `RegisterData.sol`:

   ```typescript
   export const SEPOLIA = {
     chainSelector: 16015286601757825753n,
     routerAddress: "0x0BF3dE8c5D3e8A2B34D2BEeB17ABfCeBaf363A59",
     rmnProxyAddress: "0xba3f6251de62dED61Ff98590cB2fDf6871FbB991",
     registryModuleOwnerCustomAddress: "0xa3c796d480638d7476792230da1E2ADa86e031b0",
     tokenAdminRegistryAddress: "0x95F29FEE11c5C55d26cCcf1DB6772DE953B37B82",
   } as const
   ```

2. Verifies the lane is the CCIP 2.0 lane the test expects. The test fails with a clear message if the pinned block or the lane is not what it describes:

   ```typescript
   const onRamp = await sepolia.publicClient.readContract({
     address: SEPOLIA.routerAddress,
     abi: routerOnRampAbi,
     functionName: "getOnRamp",
     args: [AMOY.chainSelector],
   })
   assert.notEqual(onRamp, ZERO_ADDRESS, "Sepolia router has no OnRamp for Amoy at the pinned block")
   assert.equal(
     await sepolia.publicClient.readContract({
       address: onRamp,
       abi: typeAndVersionAbi,
       functionName: "typeAndVersion",
     }),
     "OnRamp 2.0.0",
     "Sepolia -> Amoy is not a CCIP 2.0 lane"
   )
   ```

3. Deploys the kit's Ignition module on each fork with the per-chain parameters (router, RMN proxy, registries):

   ```typescript
   return (await fork.connection.ignition.deploy(module, {
     parameters: {
       $global: {
         routerAddress: fork.details.routerAddress,
         armProxy: fork.details.rmnProxyAddress,
         registryModuleOwnerCustom: fork.details.registryModuleOwnerCustomAddress,
         tokenAdminRegistry: fork.details.tokenAdminRegistryAddress,
         thresholdAmountForAdditionalCCVs: THRESHOLD,
       },
     },
   })) as Record<string, { address: Address }>
   ```

### Send and route the message

The `sendAndRoute()` helper shows the two-step flow used by every fork test:

1. On the source fork, run the book's send task. It builds an `ExtraArgsV3` message and calls `ccipSend` through the Sepolia router:

   ```typescript
   await quietly(() =>
     sendAction(
       {
         sourceRouter: SEPOLIA.routerAddress,
         destinationChainSelector: AMOY.chainSelector,
         receiver: forks.receiver,
         tokenToSend: token,
         amount,
         gasLimit: EOA_RECEIVER_GAS_LIMIT,
         blockConfirmations,
         feeTokenAddress: ZERO_ADDRESS,
       },
       forks.sepolia.taskHre
     )
   )
   ```

2. Fetch the `ccipSend` transaction receipt and extract the CCIP message with [`getCCIPMessages`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator-fork-js#getccipmessages), then route it on the destination connection with [`routeMessage`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator-fork-js#routemessage):

   ```typescript
   const receipt = await sepolia.connection.ethers.provider.getTransactionReceipt(sendTx.hash)
   const [sent] = getCCIPMessages(sepolia.connection, receipt)
   return routeMessage(amoy.connection, AMOY.routerAddress, sent)
   ```

   `getCCIPMessages` parses the send event for every CCIP era and returns a `CCIPSentMessage` (for CCIP 2.0, the raw `encodedMessage` and the receipts). `routeMessage` finds the destination OffRamp that serves the lane, points owner-configurable CCV resolvers at a synthetic no-op verifier, and executes the message through the OffRamp's permissionless `execute`. It returns `{ offRamp, executed, reason }` and throws if no OffRamp serves the lane or the execution fails (receiver revert, finality or CCV rejection).

   When the destination chain has a dedicated CCIP 2.0 router, pass both routers so both routers' OffRamps are searched. For example, when the destination is Ethereum Sepolia, which has a dedicated CCIP 2.0 router:

   ```typescript
   routeMessage(sepolia.connection, [SEPOLIA.routerAddress, CCIP_V2_ROUTERS[11155111]], sent)
   ```

### Faster Than Finality across the lane

The `send with Faster Than Finality delivers after both pools opt in` test case shows the CCIP 2.0 finality gates on a real lane:

1. New pools allow full finality only, so any block-depth request is rejected by the pool. The test first asserts the pool's default and expects the send to revert.

2. Opt both pools in by setting their allowed finality config (through the kit's `Example06-SetPoolFinality` task), then find the smallest depth the live lane accepts by quoting `getFee` for candidate depths:

   ```typescript
   export async function findLaneFtfDepth(forks: Forks, token: Address): Promise<number> {
     for (const depth of [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100]) {
       /* quote getFee with blockConfirmations: depth; return the first depth that does not revert */
     }
   }
   ```

3. Send with the custom finality (`blockConfirmations = depth`) and route. The transfer burns on the source and mints on the destination, same as the default-finality case, but delivered before full finality.

## What the fork helper does not model

Not modelled by the helper (and not asserted in the kit's fork tests): real CCV attestations, RMN and executor fees. CCVs on the lane are replaced by a synthetic verifier, and a manual execution does not charge the executor fee a real one costs. Pinned state never sees testnet upgrades, so green tests only prove the examples against that snapshot; re-pin the fork blocks when the lane's behavior changes or on every `@chainlink/contracts-ccip` or `@chainlink/local` bump.

## Next steps

- The other fork tests cover Lock & Release pools with a lock box (`Example07.fork.test.ts`), `AdvancedPoolHooks` (`Example08`-`Example10`). For pool-required CCVs on `AdvancedPoolHooks` in Foundry fork tests, read the [pool-based CCVs tutorial](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/pool-based-ccvs-fork).
- For the full CCT enabling procedure with the kit's tasks and Ignition modules, read the [CCT burn and mint tutorial](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/foundry/cct-burn-and-mint-fork) (the flow is the same in Hardhat; the kit's book chapters list the Hardhat task commands).
- For an index of every kit example and where its topic is documented, read the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples).

# Using Chainlink Local simulator in your Hardhat project
Source: https://docs.chain.link/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator

> **NOTE: Integrate Chainlink Local into your project**
>
> ### npm
>
> If you use [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> npm install @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### yarn
>
> If you use [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/), install the [@chainlink/local NPM
> package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainlink/local):
>
> ```shell
> yarn add @chainlink/local@0.3.1
> ```
>
> ### foundry
>
> If you use [Foundry](https://book.getfoundry.sh/):
>
> ```shell
> forge install smartcontractkit/chainlink-local@v0.3.1
> ```
>
> and then set remappings to: `@chainlink/local/=lib/chainlink-local/` in either `remappings.txt` or `foundry.toml` file
>
> ### RemixIDE
>
> Import the `CCIPLocalSimulator` contract from the `@chainlink/local` package:
>
> ```solidity
> import {CCIPLocalSimulator} from "@chainlink/local@0.3.1/src/ccip/CCIPLocalSimulator.sol";
> ```

You can use Chainlink Local to run CCIP 2.0 in a localhost environment within your Hardhat project. To get started quickly, you will use the
[CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat). This project is a Hardhat 3 boilerplate that includes the Chainlink Local
package (V3, `v0.3.1`) and CCIP 2.0 examples (`Example01`-`Example10`) as Hardhat tasks and Ignition modules.

In local mode, the simulator delivers messages synchronously inside `ccipSend` and applies the CCIP 2.0 OnRamp and OffRamp message rules: finality, one token per message, no zero amounts, and receiver CCV config validation. Read [CCIP 2.0 behavior in local mode](/chainlink-local/learn/ccip-v2-local) for the full list of what is and is not enforced.

> **NOTE: Hardhat 3 required**
>
> Chainlink Local `0.3.x` does not compile under Hardhat 2 (the contracts use `@openzeppelin/contracts@4.8.3`-style
> imports that Hardhat 2 cannot resolve, `HH411`). Hardhat 2 users stay on the `0.2.x` line (`npm install
>   @chainlink/local@0.2.9`).

## Prerequisites

1. In a terminal, clone the [CCIP Hardhat Starter Kit](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat) repository and change directories:

   ```shell
   git clone https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-starter-kit-hardhat.git && \
   cd ./ccip-starter-kit-hardhat/
   ```

2. Install the dependencies, including the [Chainlink Local](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/chainlink-local) package:

   ```shell
   npm install
   ```

3. Compile the contracts:

   ```shell
   npx hardhat build
   ```

The kit pins `solc 0.8.26` with `evmVersion: "cancun"` in `hardhat.config.ts`. CCIP 2.0 contracts need Cancun opcodes, so keep that setting in your own project. Contracts from npm packages (including the Chainlink Local simulator) are only compiled if listed in `solidity.npmFilesToBuild`.

## Test token transfers

You will run a test that transfers tokens between two accounts using `ExtraArgsV3` with Fast Transfers (non-zero block confirmations). The test file `Example01.test.ts` is located in the `./test` directory. It calls the real `example01` task action (`tasks/Example01.ts`) against the Chainlink Local simulator, so a regression in the task fails the test. The file contains four test cases:

1. **Transfer with native fees**: Transfers CCIP-BnM from the sender to a receiver EOA, paying the fee in native gas, and verifies the receiver was credited and the router collected the fee.
2. **Transfer with LINK fees**: Same transfer, paying the fee in LINK.
3. **Revert on zero amount**: The task rejects a zero amount before sending anything.
4. **Revert on zero receiver**: The task rejects a zero receiver.

For a detailed explanation of the test file, refer to the [Examine the code](#examine-the-code) section.

In your terminal, run the following command to execute the test:

```shell
npx hardhat test nodejs
```

Example output:

```text
$ npx hardhat test nodejs

Example01
  ✔ transfers token to an EOA paying the fee in native (1048ms)
  ✔ transfers token to an EOA paying the fee in LINK (166ms)
  ✔ rejects a zero amount before sending anything (105ms)
  ✔ rejects a zero receiver (96ms)

...

51 passing (3392ms)
```

No RPC URLs or keys are needed: the tests in `test/` run against the in-process Chainlink Local simulator.

## Examine the code

### Setup

The shared setup lives in `test/utils/localSimulator.ts`. Each call to `setupLocalSimulator()` returns an isolated in-process chain with the simulator deployed:

1. Connect to the in-process network and deploy the [Chainlink Local simulator](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#cciplocalsimulator) contract:

   ```typescript
   const connection = await hre.network.connect()
   const { viem } = connection
   const simulator = await viem.deployContract("CCIPLocalSimulator")
   ```

2. Read the simulator's [`configuration`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#configuration) and connect to the router, LINK and CCIP-BnM contracts:

   ```typescript
   const [chainSelector, routerAddress, , , linkAddress, bnmAddress] = await simulator.read.configuration()

   const router = await viem.getContractAt("CCIPLocalRouter", routerAddress)
   const link = await viem.getContractAt("LinkToken", linkAddress)
   const ccipBnM = await viem.getContractAt("BurnMintERC677Helper", bnmAddress)
   ```

   **Note**: The [`configuration`](/chainlink-local/api-reference/v0.3.1/ccip-local-simulator#configuration) call also returns the destination router, WETH9 and CCIP-LnM contracts, which these tests do not use. Hence, there are empty slots in the destructured array.

3. The example tasks open their own connection with `hre.network.connect()`, which would be a fresh chain. The setup hands them an hre whose `connect()` returns the test's connection instead, and exposes the first Hardhat wallet as `broadcaster` (the account every example task sends from):

   ```typescript
   const taskHre = Object.create(hre, { network: { value: { connect: async () => connection } } }) as typeof hre
   ```

4. `Example01`'s `beforeEach` funds the broadcaster with CCIP-BnM and picks the receiver:

   ```typescript
   s = await setupLocalSimulator()
   receiver = s.other.account.address
   await s.ccipBnM.write.drip([s.broadcaster.account.address])
   ```

### Test case 1: Transfer with native fees

The `transfers token to an EOA paying the fee in native` test case:

1. Set the fee the local router charges. The local router charges only what `router.write.setFee(...)` sets (default 0) and uses a mock message ID:

   ```typescript
   const fee = 10n ** 16n
   await s.router.write.setFee([fee])
   const senderBefore = await s.ccipBnM.read.balanceOf([s.broadcaster.account.address])
   ```

2. Run the task with the router, chain selector, receiver, token, amount, gas limit, block confirmations and fee token. The constants used:

   ```typescript
   const AMOUNT = 10n ** 17n
   const EOA_GAS_LIMIT = 0
   const BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS = 5
   ```

   - `EOA_GAS_LIMIT` is `0` because the receiver is an EOA: there is no `ccipReceive` logic to execute. The sender is billed for the specified gas limit, not actual usage, so do not set a gas limit for token-only transfers.
   - `BLOCK_CONFIRMATIONS` is `5` (any value `> 0`): this requests a Fast Transfer, delivered before full chain finality. `0` would mean default finality.

   ```typescript
   await run()
   ```

   where `run()` calls the task action with `feeTokenAddress: ZERO_ADDRESS` and the test's `taskHre`.

3. Inside the task, the `ExtraArgsV3` are encoded with the `encodeV3Basic` helper (`scripts/CallEncodeExtraArgsOffchain.ts`), and the [Client.EVM2AnyMessage](/ccip/evm/api-reference/v2.0.0/client#evm2anymessage) is built with the receiver, token amounts, extraArgs and fee token:

   ```typescript
   const params: EncodeV3Params = { gasLimit, blockConfirmations }
   const extraArgs = await encodeV3Basic(params)

   const ccipMessage = {
     receiver: receiverEncoded,
     data: "0x" as `0x${string}`,
     tokenAmounts,
     extraArgs,
     feeToken: feeTokenAddress,
   }
   ```

   `encodeV3Basic` maps `blockConfirmations` to the `requestedFinalityConfig` with `FinalityCodec._encodeBlockDepth`. Read more about `extraArgs` formats in the [CCIP best practices](/ccip/evm/concepts/best-practices#using-extraargs).

4. The task quotes the fee, approves the router to spend the token, and sends. With `feeTokenAddress` set to the zero address the fee is paid in native gas:

   ```typescript
   const fee = await publicClient.readContract({
     address: sourceRouter,
     abi: routerArtifact.abi,
     functionName: "getFee",
     args: [destinationChainSelector, ccipMessage],
   })
   ```

5. The test verifies the transfer: the receiver was credited, the sender was debited, and the router collected the fee. Because local mode delivers synchronously inside `ccipSend`, the assertions run immediately after the task:

   ```typescript
   assert.equal(await s.ccipBnM.read.balanceOf([receiver]), AMOUNT)
   assert.equal(await s.ccipBnM.read.balanceOf([s.broadcaster.account.address]), senderBefore - AMOUNT)
   assert.equal(await s.publicClient.getBalance({ address: s.router.address }), fee)
   ```

### Test case 2: Transfer with LINK fees

The `transfers token to an EOA paying the fee in LINK` test case runs the same task with two differences:

1. Fund the broadcaster with LINK from the simulator faucet instead of relying on native gas:

   ```typescript
   await s.simulator.write.requestLinkFromFaucet([s.broadcaster.account.address, 10n ** 18n])
   ```

2. Pass the LINK token address as the fee token (`run({ feeTokenAddress: s.link.address })`), and verify the router collected the fee in LINK:

   ```typescript
   assert.equal(await s.link.read.balanceOf([s.router.address]), fee)
   ```

### Revert test cases

The remaining two test cases verify the task's argument validation, which mirrors the CCIP 2.0 send-time rules:

1. A zero amount is rejected before anything is sent, and no tokens move:

   ```typescript
   await assert.rejects(run({ amount: 0n }), /Required args must be non-zero/)
   assert.equal(await s.ccipBnM.read.balanceOf([receiver]), 0n)
   ```

2. A zero receiver is rejected the same way:

   ```typescript
   await assert.rejects(run({ receiver: ZERO_ADDRESS }), /Required args must be non-zero/)
   ```

## Next steps

- Send a data-only message to a receiver contract and see the local router enforce its CCV config and minimum block depth in the [receiver CCV config guide](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/data-messages-receiver-ccv-config).
- For the other test files in the `./test` directory (`Example03.test.ts` programmable token transfers, `Example04.test.ts` sender contract, `Example05.test.ts` manual execution path), see the [CCIP starter kit examples map](/chainlink-local/learn/starter-kit-examples).
- To learn how to use Chainlink Local in forked environments,
  refer to the guide on [Using Chainlink Local Simulator in your Hardhat project with forked environments](/chainlink-local/build/ccip/hardhat/local-simulator-fork).
